case_name: New Brunswick School District Non. 15 v. New Brunswick (Human Rights Board of Inquiry)
text:
New Brunswick School Dist. No. 15 v. New Brunswick (Human Rights Board of Inquiry)

1989-01-19

New Brunswick Queen's Bench — Trial Division Decision under the
NEW BRUNSWICK HUMAN RIGHTS ACT, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. H-11

The Board of School Trustees, District No. 15

Applicant

v.

Human Rights Board of Inquiry, David Attis, Human Rights Commission,
Department of Education, Malcolm Ross, New Brunswick Teachers' Federation

Respondents

and

The New Brunswick Teachers' Federation

Applicant

v.

Brian D. Bruce and The Minister of Labour for the Province of New Brunswick

Respondents

Date of Decision:

January 19, 1989

Before:

Miller J.

Court Action Nos.:

M/M/278/88 and M/M/279/88

Appearances by:

James C. Letcher, Counsel for the Board of School Trustees

Eugene J. Mocker and David R. Oley, Counsel for the New Brunswick Teachers' Federation

Joanne E. MacLeod and Thomas S. Kuttner, Counsel for Human Rights Commission

Clyde Spinney, Counsel for Minister of Education

Joseph Weir, Counsel for David Attis

Gabriel Bourgeois, Counsel for Minister of Labour

Malcolm Ross on his own behalf

APPEALS AND JUDICIAL REVIEW — application to prevent hearing complaint by way of prohibition — PARTIES — complainant(s) not person directly discriminated against — PUBLIC SERVICES AND FACILITIES — discriminatory treatment in public school — definition of public services and facilities

Summary:
On application by the Board of School Trustees, District No. 15, the Court of Queen's Bench orders that a Board of Inquiry appointed to hear and decide the complaint of David Attis against the Trustees be quashed.

David Attis, who is Jewish, filed a complaint under the New Brunswick Human Rights Act alleging that the Board of School Trustees of District No. 15 discriminated with respect to a public service because it employed Malcolm Ross, who published racist books vilifying Jews and denying that the Holocaust existed and made bigoted statements in the classroom and other places, as a teacher in its schools. Mr. Attis also alleged that the Board of Trustees failed to condemn Mr. Ross' racism and bigotry and in effect condoned it, thereby creating a discriminatoyr atmosphere in the school system for his children.

The Court rules that education is not a public service within the meaning of s. 5(1) of the New Brunswick Human Rights Act. It finds that "service"in the phrase "goods, services, facilities or accommodation customarily available to the general public" refers to such things as restaurants, service stations and public transportation as Martland J. ruled in Gay Alliance Toward Equality v. Vancouver Sun.

The Court also finds that David Attis is not an aggrieved person within the meaning of hte Act because neither he nor his children have had any contact with Malcolm Ross.

The appointment of the Board of Inquiry is quashed.

Miller J.

[
1
]    There are two applications before the Court, both seeking by way of judicial review an order of prohibition to prohibit a Board of Inquriy proceeding with a scheduled hearing into a complaint lodged by one David Attis against the Board of School Trustees, District No. 15. The complaint alleges a violation of the provisions of the
Human Rights Act,
R.S.N.B. 1973, C. H-11, s. 5.

[
2
]    The issue is in fact a very narrow one, although the briefs, arguments, references and precedents submitted to the Court indicate that all parties consider the applications of more depth and concern than a regular procedural dispute. It may fairly be said that this is but another chapter in what has come to be known, at least in media circles, as "the Malcolm Ross affair" even though Mr. Ross is not a principal player at this stage of the proceedings.

[
3
]    The alleged discrimiation which set in motion the Board of Inquiry against which an order of prohibition is sought accuses the Board of School Trustees, District No. 15, and not Mr. Ross directly.

[
4
]    New Brunswick has been recognized as a pioneer in human rights legislation having enacted its first such statute in 1967. But as reminded by Mr. Justice La Forest in
Lodger's International Ltd.
v.
O'Brien,

1983 CanLII 2844 (NB CA)
,
45 N.B.R. (2d) 342
, this legislation was in a large part a re-enactment of two earlier statutes. These were the
Fair Employment Practices Act,
S.N.B. 1956, c. 9, and the
Fair Accommodation Practices Act,
S.N.B. 1959, c. 6.

[
5
]
Section 2
of the
Fair Accommodation Practices Act
provided:

2.              No person shall deny to any person or class of persons the accommodation, services or facilities available in any place to which the public is customarily admitted only because of the race, creed, colour, nationality, ancestry or place of origin of such person or class of persons.

[
6
]    The above quoted s. 2 of that statute became s . 3(6) of the
Human Rights Act,
S.N.B. 1967, c. 13, which reads:

(6)    No person shall deny to any person or class of persons the
accommodation, services of facilities
available in any place to which the public is customarily admitted only because of the race, creed, colour, nationality, ancestry or place of origin of such person or class of persons. [Emphasis added.]

[
7
]    It might be noted here that this 1967 statute, while it was binding on the Crown, was not of universal application because it did not apply to "any domestic employed in a private home" nor to a variety of organizations and non-profit organizations. It seems particularly interesting that among the groups excluded from the human rights umbrella was "any organization or corporation that is operated primarily to foster the welfare of a religious or racial group . . ."

[
8
]    In 1972 the
Human Rights Act
[S.N.B., c. 8] was extensvely amended and for the first time the worthy principles of the statute were set forth in the preamble. It is stated,
inter alia,
"it is recognized that human rights must be guaranteed by the rule of law . . ." It must be presumed that the
Act
recognizes that the rule of law governs and protects the accuser as well as the accused.

It was in this 1971 amendment that the legislature considerably expanded the protection afforded by the human rights legislation.

In that amended
Act
is found a provision directly relating to the occupation of commercial and residential properties.

[
9
]    Section 4(1) provides:

(1)    No person directly or indirectly, alone or with another, by himself or by the interposition of another, shall

(a)      deny to any person or class of persons the right to occupy any commercial unit or dwelling unit; or

(b)      discriminate against any person or class of persons with respect to any term or condition of occupancy of any commercial unit or any dwelling unit;

because of race, colour, religion, national origin, ancestry or place of origin.

[
10
]    Section 5 was introduced in the following terms:

5.              No person, directly or indirectly, alone or with another, by himself or by the interposition of another, shall

(a)      deny to any person or class of persons the
accommodation, services, or facilities
available in any place to which the public is customarily admitted; or

(b)      discriminate against any person or class of persons with respect to the accommodations, services, or facilities available in any place to which the public is customarily admitted;

because of race, colour, religion, national origin, ancestry or place of origin. [Emphasis added.]

Then in 1985 the
Act
was again the subject of a major re-structuring [S.N.B., c. 30] and at this time s. 5 as we now know it appeared and it is this section which gives rise to the matter now under consideration.

Section 5 now reads:

(1)    No person, directly or indirectly, alone or with another, by himself or by the interposition of another, shall

(a)      deny to any person or class of persons any
accommodation, services or facilities
available to the public, or

(b)      discriminate against any person or class of persons with respect to any accommodation, services or facilities available to the public,

because of race, colour, religion, national origin, ancestry, place of origin, age, physical disability, mental disability, marital status or sex. [Emphasis added.]

It is within this framework of the history of human rights legislation that this matter has reached the Court.

[
11
]    From the affidavit evidence which has been filed, it appears that Malcolm Ross is a teacher employed by School District No. 15 and has been so employed for several years. It also appears that Mr. Ross is an author and his books are undoubtedly the major focus of the present matter. It would not be unreasonable, because of the media attention, to take judicial notice of the fact that Mr. Ross' books have created a public controversy.

[
12
]    On January 29, 1987, the District 15 School Board established a committee "to enquire into the possible impact of the alleged private actions of Mr. Malcolm Ross upon the learning environment in school programs."

[
13
]    In what appears to be the result of a thorough and comprehensive study and investigation, the committee unanimously concluded:

(1)    That there appears to be no evidence to suggest that Malcolm Ross is teaching his beliefs or discussing his religious theories with staff or students.

(2)    That there is not [
sic
] evidence to suggest that the publicity surrounding Malcolm Ross has had a negative effect on the human relations within the present school or between the school and the community.

[
14
]    Despite the findings of its special committee, the School Board on March 1, 1988, adopted the following motion:

Moved by P. Crossan, seconded by S. Murray, that Mr. Malcolm Ross be informed that:

a)    The Board of School Trustees strongly disapproves of his continued publication of materials expressing controversial views and reprimands him for such activities as have inhibited the employer's ability to efficiently manage and direct the educational process.

b)    Any further publications or engaging in any public forum or discussion of his views, or in relation to his publications, now or in the future, will result in more severe disciplinary action by the Board of School Trustees including the possibility of dismissal.

c)    His compliance with directive "b" above will result in the Board considering this matter closed.

[
15
]    By a document dated April 21, 1988, David Attis, one of the parties herein, filed with the New Brunswick Human Rights Commission a "complaint" as contemplated by s. 17 of the
Human Rights Act,
which reads:

Any person claiming to be aggrieved because of an alleged violation of this Act may make a complaint in writing to the Commission in a form prescribed by the Commission.

The form is obviously provided by the Commission although the complaint was drafted and filed without legal advice.

[
16
]    The complaint is filed against the Board of School Trustees of District No. 15, alleging discrimination under s. 5 of the statute (as set forth herein) for the period of "March 29/77 thru April 21, 1988." The terms of the complaint of David Attis are:

I am a Jew and three of my children are enrolled as students within District No. 15.

I have reason to believe that Malcolm Ross, a teacher employed by the School Board, made racist, discriminatory and bigoted statements to his students during the 1976–77 school year. I have reason to believe that the School Board knew of this, yet it merely transferred Malcolm Ross to another school.

Malcolm Ross has written at least two books (i.e.
Web of Deceit
and
Spectre of Power
) and has made widely published statements (eg.
Miramichi Leader,
October 22, 1986, page 5) that are anti-Jewish, racist, bigoted and discriminatory and that deny that six million Jews died during the Nazi Holocaust.

On April 22, 1987, the School Board failed to pass a motion condemning bigotry and racism. On March 15 and 16, 1988, Ray Maybee, a member of the School Board, publicly stated that Malcolm Ross' opinions were well documented and he had done his homework, thus appearing to support Mr. Ross' discriminatory views. Furthermore, when the School Board reprimanded Malcolm Ross on March 15, 1988, it referred to his views merely as controversial rather than discriminatory and the reprimand applied only to his future actions, not his past actions.

By its own statements and its inaction over Malcolm Ross' statements in class and in public, the School Board has condoned his views, has thus provided a racist and anti- Jewish role model for its students, has fostered a climate where students feel more at ease expressing anti-Jewish views, and has reduced the credibility of the content of its official history curriculum, thus depriving Jews and other minority students of equal opportunity within the educational system that the School Board provides as a service to the public.

I believe that the School Board has thus furthered the aims of the Ross' of our society. I would like to give a couple of examples:

i)    Several students at the Magnetic Hill School intend to present a petition to the Premier of New Brunswick in support of Malcolm Ross. When asked if they concurred with Ross' views, the students replied that they didn't know.

ii)    My eldest daughter, a grade 6 student at Beaverbrook School was invited by a friend to attend a gymnastic exhibition at Magnetic Hill School. She was reminded by a classmate that she shouldn't go there because that is "where the teacher who hates Jews" works. She attended nevertheless.

I have reasonable cause to believe that the Board of School Trustees of District No. 15 has violated Section 5 of the Human Rights Act.

[
17
]    By s. 18 of the
Act
the Commission is required "to inquire into any complaint made pursuant to section 17 and shall endeavour to effect a settlement of the matter complained of."

[
18
]    The material filed indicates that the investigation officer appointed to the case instituted the inquiry and there is no reason to suspect that it followed other than a normal routine. On June 30, 1988, the officer (Francis Young) wrote to the Superintendent of School District No. 15 concerning the matter and said:

The objectives of our investigation will be to determine if David Attis' school age children and . . . have been subjected to anti-Jewish discrimination since March, 1987 and, if so, whether it can be linked to the actions or statements of the Board of School Trustees of District 15 and its employees, Malcolm Ross in particular.

[
19
]    He then outlined what he anticipated to be the necessary steps in his investigation. The intended inquiry could only be described as exhaustive and time-consuming, involving numerous interviews with school officials, teachers and students.

[
20
]    There is no documentation before me to indicate the progress of the inquiry. There is on file a document that purports to be the terms of a proposed settlement of the complaint.

[
21
]    There is, however, a report "update" of August 31, 1988, in which Mr. Young states that:

The officer met with Carl Ross, the Chairman of the School Board, Cheryl Reid, the Acting Superintendent, Mrs. Lutz, Vice-Chairman and James Letcher, the Board's lawyer, on August 3, 1988 to discuss conciliation of the Attis and the . . . complaints.

It is further stated:

In the meantime, the officer has pursued other avenues of investigation. On August 24, the officer met with Carl Ross to discuss the Board's official response to the Attis and . . . complaints and to get background information for the investigation of the complaints. The Board has authorized Malcolm Ross to speak to the officer and the officer will attempt to meet him.

This comment was apparently written by Mr. Young August 31, 1988.

[
22
]    Malcolm Ross filed an affidavit which indicates that on the same date Dr. Noel Kinsella, then Chairman of the Human Rights Commission, was quoted on a television news report as saying among other things that: "Ross could be out of the classroom before he corrects his Christmas exams."

The Commission has not replied to nor refuted this allegation of Mr. Ross.

[
23
]    The very next day, September 1, 1988, Dr. Kinsella, as Chairman of the Commission, recommended to the Minister of Labour that a board of inquiry be appointed to inquire into this complaint as provided for by s. 20 of the
Act.

[
24
]    It should be noted that by s. 18(2) of the
Act,
the Commission may dismiss the complaint if in its opinion the complaint is without merit. Obviously the investigation was still in progress one day before the Commission recommended a board of inquiry. Section 20 provides for such a Board "if the Commission is unable to effect a settlement of the matter complained of. . . ."

[
25
]    With commendable alacrity, on the same date as the recommendation was made — September 1, 1988 — the Minister appointed Professor Brian D. Bruce as the Board of Inquiry.

[
26
]    Later Professor Bruce named six parties to appear before the Board of Inquiry, all of whom appeared on this application. The Board was scheduled to hold its first meeting November 21, 1988. The Board has not met, pending the outcome of these applications.

[
27
]    A fundamental issue addressed by the parties was the propriety of an application for an order of prohibition. Although all parties are not in agreement, I consider that there can be no question that the court can in appropriate circumstances order that an established administrative board be prohibited from acting.

[
28
]    I am equally satisfied that this power should only be exercised with extreme caution. Non-judicial tribunals have a properly recognized role and their functions should not be usurped or interfered with except where it is clear that the court should interfere on a matter of law.

[
29
]    Despite the arguments of some counsel I am satisfied that the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in
Bell
v.
Ontario Human Rights Commission,

1971 CanLII 195 (SCC)
,
[1971] S.C.R. 756
, is still good law
and binding on this Court.

[
30
]    It was there [p. 775] held by Mr. Justice Martland speaking for the majority that:

In my opinion the appellant was not compelled to await the decision of the board on that issue before seeking to have it determined in a court of law by an application for prohibition, and the Court had jurisdiction to deal with the matter.

[
31
]    Therefore it follows that if the applicants herein can properly raise an issue of law then they have followed a propre course in seeking an order or prohibition by way of judicial review.

[
32
]    At the same time great care must be taken as reminded by Chief Justice Culltion in
Re CIP Paper Products Ltd. and Saskatchewan Human Rights Commission

(1978),
1978 CanLII 1847 (SK CA)
,
87 D.L.R. (3d) 609 (Sask. C.A.)
, that rights and duties statutorily assigned to a commission should not be usurped by the court under the guise of prohibition proceedings.

[
33
]    There are now many reported cases dealing with human rights legislation at both federal and provincial levels. This has been a rapidly expanding field, as all legislatures have become acutely aware of the need or protection for the rights and dignity of all citizens without distinction.

[
34
]    Insofar as I am aware, no court has considered the origin of the combined words of "accommodation, services and facilities" as found in s. 5 of the New Brunswick statute and in most other similar statutes.

[
35
]    In this province, the expression clearly emanates from the
Fair Accommodation Practices Act
and within the framework of that statute I would not consider it difficult in determining the limits of the anti-discriminatory measures.

Generally speaking and particularly in New Brunswick legislatures have not seen fit to expand the limits of this protection.

[
36
]    In
Gay Alliance Toward Equality
v.
Vancouver Sun

(1979),
1979 CanLII 225 (SCC)
,
97 D.L.R. (3d) 577
, the Supreme Court of Canada considered whether the refusal of an advertisement submitted by a homosexual association was a violation of human rights legislation which protected against denial "to any person or class of persons any accommodation, service, or facility customarily available to the public."

[
37
]    Martland J. for the majority said [p. 590]:

In my opinion the general purpose of s. 3 was to prevent discrimination against individuals or groups of individuals in respect of the provision of certain things available generally to the public. The items dealt with are similar to those covered by legislation in the United States, both federal and state. "Accommodation" refers to such matters as accommodation in hotels, inns and motels. "Service" refers to such matters as restaurants, bars, taverns, service stations, public transportation and public utilities. "Facility" refers to such matters as public parks and recreational facilities. These are all items "customarily available to the public." It is matters such as these which have been dealt with in American case law on the subject of civil rights.

[
38
]    Mr. Justice Kroft in
Re Winnipeg School Division No. 1 and MacArthur

(1982),
1982 CanLII 2975 (MB QB)
,
133 D.L.R. (3d) 305
, [
1982 CanLII 4893 (MB QB)
,
3 C.H.R.R. D/917
] (Man. Q.B.), followed this decision and held that a public school does not fall within the term "accommodation, service or facility customarily available to the public" as is found in the
Human Rights Act
of Manitoba.

[
39
]    In
Insurance Corp. of British Columbia
v.
Heerspink

(1982),
1982 CanLII 27 (SCC)
,
137 D.L.R. (3d) 219
, [3 C.H.R.R. D/1163] the Supreme Court of Canada again considered the same matter but in an indirect way. In this case an insurer had cancelled a policy of insurance because the assured had been charged with a narcotics offence and purportedly within the contractual conditions of the policy.

[
40
]    The question was whether such a contractual condition violated the human rights legislation. The issue was whether the insurer had "reasonable cause" for such cancellation. The majority of the Court held that the matter of "unreasonable cause" is a question of fact and therefore the case was not a proper one for the appeal process.

[
41
]    However, Martland J., who dissented from the majority decision, held that the termination of the contract of insurance was not a denial of service.

[
42
]    Mr. Justice Lamer, on the other hand, who concurred with the majority decision, said, "I can see no reason why insurance was not intended by the Legislature to be a ”˜service' in the sense in which the word is used in s. 3 of the Code." (The s. 3 of the
Code
to which Mr. Justice Lamer referred was the same section dealt with in the
Gay Alliance
case, which concerned the expression "accommodation, service or facility customarily available to the public.")

[
43
]    More recent cases seem to follow a path of expansion of the meaning of statutory words, thereby widening the protective net of human rights legislation.

[
44
]    The Federal Court of Canada has opened this door in a case reported as
Re Singh

(1988),
1988 CanLII 5665 (FCA)
,
86 N.R. 69
, [
1988 CanLII 8967 (FCA)
,
10 C.H.R.R. D/5501
]. The Appeal Court discussed the effect of s. 5 of the
Canadian Human Rights Act,
S.C. 1976–77, c. 33, as it related to the operations of the immigration service of the Department of External Affairs.

[
45
]    The said s. 5 of the federal statute states:

5.              It is a discriminatory practice in the provision of goods, services, facilities or accommodation customarily available to the general public

(a)      to deny, or to deny access to, any such good, service, facility or accommodation to any individual, or

(b)      to differentiate adversely in relation to any individual,

on a prohibited ground of discrimination.

[
46
]    Mr. Justice Hugessen, without deciding the issue, said it is arguable that, "by definition, services rendered by public servants at public expense are services to the public and therefore fall within the ambit of section 5."

[
47
]    In a judgment dated June 24, 1988, [
Saskatchewan (Human Rights Commission)
v.
Saskatchewan (Department of Social Services),

1988 CanLII 212 (SK CA)
,
9 C.H.R.R. D/5181
] the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal decided that social assistance benefits was a "service" within the provision of "accommodation, services or facilities to which the public is customarily admitted or which are offered to the public" as set forth in
s. 12(1)
of
The
Saskatchewan Human Rights Code,
S.S. 1979, c. S-24.1.

[
48
]    In that case, Vancise J.A. referred to several cases in which a variety of public services have been held to be included in the expression of services offered or available to the public.

[
49
]    There is no doubt in my mind that the judicial pendulum has swung to an inclusive position that "services," whatever they are, are included in the human rights protective legislation unless it can be shown that a particular service is not so included.

[
50
]    Mr. Justice Martland in the
Gay Alliance
case said that the word "service" as used in the
Human Rights Act
included such things as "restaurants, bars, taverns, service stations, public transportation and public utilities." It is an abuse of language to add to that list other classifications as maternity benefits, policing, insurance, income equalization payment and immigration procedures.

[
51
]    There is no valid reason why the human rights legislative protection should not or could not be extended to include all these other categories but that, in my opinion, is a function and decision that rests with the legislature and not with the courts.

[
52
]    If the word "services" stood alone in s. 5(1) of the
Human Rights Act
I would have no difficulty in accepting an extensive and all-inclusive meaning of the term. But coupled with the words "accommodation" and "facilities" I am of the opinion that the meaning and application of "services" is limited as described by the Supreme Court of Canada in the
Gay Alliance
case. That decisoin has not been reversed and with respect I agree with the conclusion.

[
53
]    It is therefore myopinion that the provisoin of school facilities and an educational program is not included within the meaning of "accommodation, services and facilities" as found in s. 5 of the
Human Rights Act
of New Brunswick.

[
54
]    The applicants raise a further issue which I believe relates directly to the jurisdiction of the Board of Inquiry.

The whole proceeding has been based on an allegation of discrimination. Section 17 of the
Human Rights Act,
above quoted, refers to a complaint by a person aggrieved on a form prescribed by the Commission. This form refers to "Type of Discrimination," "Date or period of offence" and "Basis of Discrimination."

[
55
]    Some of these words and terms must be examined, for they are not defined in the statute.

There can be no doubt that human rights legislation should be given a broad interpretation to ensure that the stated objects and purposes are fulfilled. This approach has been consistently declared and followed by many courts.

[
56
]    However, it does not follow that accused violators of human rights do not have rights to be protected. Nor does it mean that there is any particular magic to the words "human rights" which would allow all normal procedural rules and legal principles to be abandoned.

[
57
]    The New Brunswick Court of Appeal considered the matter of a "complaint" in
Mackin
v.
Judicial Council (N.B.)

(1987),
1987 CanLII 138 (NB CA)
,
82 N.B.R. (2d) 203
. In that case the Attorney General of the Province lodged a complaint against a judge of the Provincial Court. The Judicial Council directed that an inquiry be held as provided for in the
Provincial Court Act,
R.S.N.B. 1973, c. P-21.

[
58
]    The text of the Attorney General's letter of complaint is set out in full in the Report. It was this document that was considered by the Court of Appeal on an application by way of judicial review for an order of prohibition.

Hoyt J.A. said [p. 220]:

A complaint . . . must be expressed in clear terms . . .

It [the complaint] is imprecise in its allegations and is nothing more than a request for the Judicial Council to investigate and see whether it could uncover misconduct, neglect of duty or inability . . . to perform his duties.

[
59
]    Mr. Justice Hoyt (with whom Angers J.A. agreed) said that the requirements for a specific complaint is two-fold.

Not only must the Judicial Council know what they are being asked to consider but the Judge against whom the complaint is made must know what allegations he faces.

[
60
]    In my opinion the same principles should apply to protect other citizens — in this case a school board. And to substitute only the parties I would with respect agree that in this case:

Not only must the Board of Inquiry (Professor Bruce) know what it is being asked to consider, but the School Board against whom the complaint is made must know what allegations it faces.

[
61
]    The Attis complaint refers to "racial, discriminatory and bigoted statements" made by Malcolm Ross during the 1976–77 school year and the School Board, with knowledge of these statements, merely transferred Ross to another school.

There is no indication in all the reports of the Commission's investigation that these alleged statements were ever identified or communicated to the School Board.

[
62
]    A question has been raised as to whether David Attis can make a representative complaint because he alleges that the School Board has deprived "Jewish and other minority students of equal opportunity within the educational system."

[
63
]    David Attis is a member of the Jewish community within School District 15, but the evidence is that neither he nor his children have ever had contact with Mr. Ross as a teacher.

[
64
]    The
Act
says that an aggrieved person may make a complaint. Webster's
New Collegiate Dictionary
defines "aggrieved" in the legal sense as:

suffering from an infringement or denial of legal rights.

[
65
]    In
Re Saskatchewan Human Rights Commission and Canadian Odeon Theatres Ltd.,

1985 CanLII 183 (SK CA)
,
18 D.L.R. (4th) 93 (Sask. C.A.)
[leave to appeal to S.C.C. refused June 3, 1985], Vancise J.A. defined "discrimination" as follows [p. 115]:

Discrimination in a human rights context is exclusion, restriction or preference of treatment based on one of a number of protected characteristics the result of which is the prevention or impairment of the exercise of human rights and freedoms guaranteed in the Code.

If this be a proper definition of "discrimination" within the terms of the
Human Rights Act,
and I accept that it is, I fail to see that there is even a suggestion of discrimination in this sense on the part of the School Board.

[
66
]    It seems obvious that David Attis is dissatisfied and disenchanted with the School Board for its failure to implement satisfactory sanctions against Malcolm Ross. It is equally obvious that the Chairman of the Human Rights Commission desired the same results as Mr. Attis.

[
67
]    This application does not directly concern Malcolm Ross, his teaching, which has been praised, or his private views and writings, which have been condemned. Whether he should or should not be a school teacher is not the immediate concern in this application nor has this issue been addressed.

[
68
]    It must be obvious that no elected body of citizens can ever achieve complete approval of its constituency. Such is the case with the School Board.

[
69
]    It is possible within the scheme or the provisions of the
Human Rights Act
that a body such as the School Board could be guilty of discriminatory practices in violation of that
Act.

[
70
]    But the board of inquiry authorized by the legislation can only be set in motion by a proper complaint from an aggrieved party alleging discrimination within the provisions of the statute.

[
71
]    Even had I been convinced that the legislation should be so broadly interpreted as to include the educational system within the term "services" as found in s. 5 of the
Act,
I would not have been satisfied that other required standards for such an inquiry had been met.
